title: O6 – Power: Milgram, legitimacy, dependency, Crozier, French & Raven

blocks.text: Milgram: ordinary people obey a legitimate authority to the point of harming others – the “agentic state”.
Weber: people obey because they find authority legitimate – traditional, charismatic or rational-legal.
Power is not an attribute but a relationship: A's power over B grows with B's dependence on resources A controls (Emerson, Blau, Pfeffer & Salancik).
Crozier: no one is powerless; power is proportional to the capacity to create or control uncertainty for others.
French & Raven: five bases of power – formal (reward, coercive, legitimate) and personal (referent, expert).
Subjects were asked by an experimenter in a lab coat to give increasingly strong electric shocks to a “learner” (an actor).
65 % obeyed to the end · 48 % in a scruffy building · 23 % when orders came by phone · 40 % when the victim sat next to the subject.

Agentic state: the individual merely executes another's will – the disappearance of a sense of responsibility is the most far-reaching consequence of submission to authority. Rational-legal legitimacy and expertise (Yale, the lab coat) drive obedience.
Devotion to the exceptional abilities of a person – prophets, heroes, Napoleon.
Belief in the sanctity of immemorial customs, sometimes hereditary – dynasties.
Belief in the legality of impersonal rules – a police officer. Milgram's experimenter draws on rational-legal and expert authority.
Power is a relationship, constantly negotiated – not set in stone.
Controlling resources another needs gives power over them.
Power is never one-sided: the one who obeys still has power through how he complies.
Reciprocity is never equal or static; grey zones are potential sources of power.
A's power over B rises the more B needs the resource, the less B can get it elsewhere and the less B can force A. What counts is how actors perceive their needs.

Weber's view: authority flows in one direction along the hierarchy. Crozier & Friedberg (1977): power is a balance of forces; no one is completely powerless – it works in both directions through negotiation.

An individual's power is proportional to his capacity to create uncertainty concerning the execution of his tasks (Crozier, 1964): actors try to maximise their own zones of uncertainty and to control those of others.

Control of expertise (hard to replace) · control of relationships with the environment (networks, social capital) · control of communication and information flows · use of organisational rules (subordinates use rules for protection against arbitrariness; supervisors create rules or bargain over them).
Study on the Pentagon and the maintenance workers of a French state monopoly: real power can differ widely from the organisation chart.
Reward (control of valued rewards) · coercive (fear of consequences) · legitimate (formal authority from position and mutual agreement).
Referent / charismatic (others identify with or want to be like the agent) · expert (trusted, relevant expertise perceived by others).

Mission of the consulting team: diagnose the causes in banking with the course models – structure (Mintzberg), culture (Schein), incentives of the risk controllers (contribution–retribution) – and assess the proposed reform.
